utterances.text: I'd like an answer to my question, Dr. Markovski. Do you want me it repeat it one more time?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're speaking about sides. I do not agree that there have been, in this conflict, as you call it, or in the crisis in the Republic of Macedonia, sides to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, let me see if I can rephrase my question a little bit then. If both the members of the NLA and the members of the security forces of the Republic of Macedonia committed some crimes against civilians during 2001, that would, unfortunately, be one of the characteristics found in a classic armed conflict, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can't discuss a typical armed conflict when what we have here is state and legal entities, and we have armed extremist gangs, the activities of which followed the methodology of terrorism. I really can't permit, neither from a scientific nor from a practical aspect, to correlate the two and to run a parallel between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I'll use your language. Suppose, in 2001, we have some armed extremist gangs, "terrorists," to use your term, and we have the Macedonian --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said "armed extremists," the methodology of which is terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Well, suppose we have some armed extremists, in 2001, who commit abuses against civilians, and we have some members of the security forces of the Republic of Macedonia who commit abuses against civilians, wouldn't that be very similar to one of the common characteristics of an armed conflict that we talked about earlier?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not understand how you insist to ran a parallel between the two structures. Ask me separately about the one and the other, and I will answer properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to another topic, Dr. Markovski. I'd like to talk to you a little bit about the Ministry of Defence and how it works and how the army of the Republic of Macedonia works. It's my understanding that the Ministry of Defence in Macedonia traditionally deals with all aspects of defence affairs and preparations at the republic level. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the state level, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, so, that would include activities like civil defence preparations, maintaining lists of reservists, scientific research, publishing documents, et cetera, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. But I would kindly ask you to indicate where that is in my report, so that I'm able to follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I'm actually not referring to any part of your report right now. I'm just asking you to confirm -- to confirm this. The Ministry of Defence --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. Then we will speak from a theoretical viewpoint, no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And from a factual viewpoint. And in Macedonia, usually, the minister of defence has been a civilian, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Pursuant to Article 97 of the constitution, it is obligatory that the minister is a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, in 2001, the minister was a civilian named Vlado Buckovski, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, in 2001, from the creation of the broad coalition government, or coalition, Mr. Buckovski was appointed a minister. There was another minister before him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And also, within the Ministry of Defence - correct me if I'm wrong - but I believe there was another part or institution called the General Staff of the army of the Republic of Macedonia, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the Law on Defence, the General Staff is an expert body within the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And you're referring, of course, to the new Law on Defence that was enacted in the summer of 2001, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to both the new law, but I'm indicating that there were no substantial or essential amendments with regards to the old one. I'm also referring to the final provisions of the law which indicate that until the adoption of certain secondary legislation items that would support the new articles of the new Law on Defence, the old law will apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. We're going to come back, but let me ask you some more questions. I think we'll come back to this point in a minute. The General Staff of the army was composed of professional military officers, wasn't it, in 2001?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Senior officers, that would mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry the interpreters did not hear the last part of your response. Perhaps you could repeat --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters will continue the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that would mean commissioned and non-commissioned officers. I wish to be more precise than your assertion. Professional soldiers can be ordinary soldiers as well, but the General Staff is composed of commissioned and non-commissioned officers and certain number of civilians serving in the army --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "Employed" in the army, rather than "serving" in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And the normal job of the General Staff of an army is to run the army and military operations, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To plan, lead, and analyse the activities undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. After the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia broke apart during the early 1990s and Macedonia became an independent republic, there was a policy to reduce the level of militarisation of the country. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. We might come to this conclusion further in our discussions, so please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you mean, but I will go on.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is too broad a question, and I can't give you a specific answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, the role of the army, during the mid- to late 1990s in Macedonia, was reduced, wasn't it, from the time-period when the JNA existed? Would that be correct to say?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the JNA existed, the army of the Republic of Macedonia did not exist. I really do not understand you. If you are referring to the number of military officers in the Republic of Macedonia who belonged to the army of the Republic of Macedonia was smaller than the number of the officers that the JNA had in Macedonia while Yugoslavia still existed, then the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And it would be fair to say, then, a number of officers, even generals, were retired during that time. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They retired during 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, consequently, the role of the General Staff of the army of the Republic of Macedonia was also diminished, wasn't it, at that time, in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. This has nothing to do with the reduction or the retirement of certain number of generals. This can't be compared in this way. But the army was reduced according to a plan. In a planned fashion, according to the NATO standards, the transformation of the army commenced to have it more mobile; and because of the specific features of the territory of the Republic of Macedonia, the army was trained and is still trained in a planned fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Well, prior to the crisis time of 2001, one of the generals who was returned was Pande Petrovski, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're completely right. It is like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then, during the crisis time, in 2001, General Petrovski was brought back from retirement to lead the General Staff of the army of the Republic of Macedonia during the crisis. Isn't that what also what happened?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is true. This is exactly how it happened. However, the decision on the retirement of generals and their activation or reactivation was made or issued by the president, by the Supreme Commander of the armed forces. That was his political decision on the basis of the constitution and the Law on Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Now, when the crisis began in the early part of 2001, the old Law on Defence was the governing law, right, because the new law had not been enacted yet. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 6th of July, 2001, the Law on Defence of 1995 was in force or the amended version of the law which was passed in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Well, the old Law on Defence -- in the old Law on Defence, the roles and responsibility of the General Staff were not clearly defined or described, were they?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the views or interpretations. My opinion was completely different, that it was completely, precisely, and properly defined, the role of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, no, I'm not asking about the role of the army. My question was specifically directed to the role of the General Staff. My question was that in the old law, the particular duties and powers and responsibilities of the General Staff were not specifically defined. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In both the old and the new Law on Defence, General Staff is an expert body, expert and operational body of the Ministry of Defence. I don't see where you find your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Well, maybe you can help me clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can show the witness -- first of all, I need to explain something to Your Honours. A small portion of the old Law on Defence has already been admitted into evidence, and it is Exhibit 1D97. But that exhibit only contains, I believe, two, perhaps three, of the Articles of the old law. So I'm going to ask that the witness be shown 65 ter 1236, which is a more complete version. To my knowledge, it is a complete version of the old Law on Defence, because I would like to ask the witness to look at it. This can be found in binder 4, tab 127.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If it would help you, Dr. Markovski -- Dr. Markovski, if you take a look at binder 4 and go to tab 127, then you could look at a hard copy of the full version, and it might be quicker, actually.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which tab did you say, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There's an English version --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There's an English version which has not translated every Article but has translate add number of Articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you can just follow with me, Dr. Markovski, the chapter headings, we see the basic provision. I'm sorry. I'll wait for you. We see the first chapter is titled basic provision; the second chapter is titled citizen rights and duties in the defence. And, again, this is the decree on the declaration of the Law on Defence published in the Official Gazette, 14 February 1992. And we see a number of Articles about military service in chapter 2; we see the responsibilities or duties of citizens; Article 12, we see an Article regarding the needs of the army during a state of war. In chapter 3, we see the competencies of the organs of the state government, and that's divided into the Assembly of the Republic, which is Article 14; the president of the Republic, which is Article 15; and the government of the Republic, which is Article 16. Then, if you get to Article 17, we see the Ministry of Defence, and we see the different roles and responsibilities of the Ministry of Defence in Article 17. Then, if you turn to what is chapter 4, which is the chapter on the army of the Republic, we see a number of Articles that talk about the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this is on page 9 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The army is an armed force of all citizens in the Republic, that's Article 19; Article 20, the army prepares and gets qualified or trained for waging armed war and combat and other actions in a state of war; Article 21, the army organises and prepares in a state of peace in order to realise its constitutional function for defence of the Republic, et cetera. Do you see that? Are you following me, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm following you, but there is a serious criticism to be made here. You probably wish to indicate that this law is substantially different from the law of 2001; but I wish to indicate, on the contrary, that this law, passed on the 14th of February, 1992, was amended in 1995. Actually, before the crisis, and until the adoption of the new law, the Law on Defence of 1995 was in force. At this moment, I don't know; or if we have it here, maybe we could compare the amendments. I can't comment on this from the top of my head. What you are trying to, escape from the law or deviate from this law of 2001, is making me avoid this law of 1992, because what was in force was the law of 1992 but with the amendments passed in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just for the record, Dr. Markovski, I'm not trying to escape from anything. I'm trying to clarify what the situation was in Macedonia, all right? Now --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. It was not the sense in which I meant. It is not how you understood it. I spoke metaphorically because I also said that I tried to escape something as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. I do not have the 1995 amendments with me, but I need to ask you something about the 1992 law, if I may. There's nothing in the 1992 law that describes the powers and functions of the General Staff of the army of the Republic of Macedonia, is there?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is where the problem this. This is what I wish to indicate. I'm not sure at this moment that this is what is missing in 1995 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Markovski, I asked you a simple question. All you need to do is say "yes" or "no." Is there anything in the 1992 law that describes or defines the powers and responsibility of the General Staff of the army of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But how could I answer this when this law was not in force in 2001. In 2001, at the beginning of the crisis, what was in force was the law of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did the law of 1995 contain a description of the powers and responsibility of the General Staff of the army?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem is that I never learn the Articles of any law by heart. If we have it here, we could comment on this. This is what I wish to indicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So your answer is you're not sure. You're just not sure.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm absolutely not sure, because I don't have the law here to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Is it fair to say that during the crisis time, when the crisis began in the early part of 2001, there were disputes within the Ministry of Defence as to which person the minister or the chief of the General Staff should be the person in command of the army units. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if you allow me, I don't see a possibility for something like this happening, because the competencies of the chief of the General Staff is one thing, and the minister is a political person elected by the government. If you have something more specific, we might discuss it. I really don't know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if the roles were clearly described, if the role -- if the powers and responsibilities of the General Staff were clearly defined in the 1995 Law on Defence, then there would be no need to define them in the new Law on Defence that was enacted in 2001, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an assumption. I really cannot respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness what is Exhibit 1D00098, which is in binder 2, and it's tab 48. If the witness could be assisted so that he could find binder 2, and if you could go to tab 48, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You'll see, Dr. Markovski, that this is the so-called new Law on Defence that was enacted in 2001.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why so-called? This is a real law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Markovski, the reason I used the term "so-called" is because that's the term that the parties here during this trial have used in court, just to distinguish between the earlier law and the subsequent law, all right? We get through this more quickly if you could just answer the questions that I ask you, okay?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. But in the Macedonian language, the wording "so-called" bears a negative connotation. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we can, please, if you could turn, please, Dr. Markovski, to chapter 4 of the old -- excuse me, of the law that's in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It is has ERN number N002-2795.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you have chapter 4 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For those following in English, we see a chapter here called: General Staff. Subsection two of this chapter is entitled General Staff, and it begins with Article 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says that: "Operational and expert activities for organizing, preparing, and commanding the armed forces in the Ministry of Defence are accomplished by the General Staff being the highest expert body within the Ministry of Defence on issues related to the armed forces." Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I repeated this on several occasions, and I basically provided the definition that this is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in Article 26, we see the duties and responsibilities of the General Staff. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we see at least 21 separate duties and responsibilities, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, to your knowledge, was Article 26 implemented -- was Article 26 a new Article in 2001 or did it exist already in the old law?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should really take a look at this law in order to be able to say more, but let's discuss it further and see what you're after. It is very difficult for a person to know a law by heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. How about Article 27? It refers to the chief of the -- the chief manages the General Staff of the armed forces, who is appointed and discharged by the president of the Republic." "The chief of the General Staff reports to the president of the Republic and to the minister ..." Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember this was as it is, in the past and now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in 2001, then, the chief of the General Staff of the -- yeah, the chief of the General Staff was -- was managing the General Staff, right, as it says in Article 27?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the General Staff, in 2001, were carrying out the activities as described in Article 26, right, throughout the crisis time?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is how it is supposed to be, according to the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Now, during the crisis time in 2001, General Pande Petrovski was the chief of the General Staff until the 10th of August, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 9th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for correcting me. And the deputy chief of the General Staff was General Metodija Stamboliski, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, at that particular time?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And during the crisis time, while these two officers held their positions, a big part of their job was to plan the responses of the armed forces of Macedonia to the armed actions of the NLA, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot agree with this position. The chief of the General Staff and his deputy are the highest officers and the most responsible officers in the army of the Republic of Macedonia. The planning, carrying out, and the analysis are being made by their assistants and commanders of the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Let me then step back a bit. So the General, if I can -- if I can say this clearly, the General Staff is composed of general officers like Pande Petrovski and Metodija Stamboliski, as well as a group of people who work for the chief and the deputy chief, yeah, and carry out work for them. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Amongst them, Blagoja Markovski, as a colonel, was also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So amongst the staff of the General Staff would be people who would plan operations and present those plans to General Petrovski and General Stamboliski for their approval. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the General Staff, in 2001, considering that it was organised or structured according to the NATO standards, there was the so-called G3, and this G3 service is the service for planning of operations. But this department or service did not present its plans to the chief and the deputy chief only, but at the collegium of the General Staff. The General Staff is a collective body managing the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And at the collegium, when these plans were presented, people like General Petrovski and General Stamboliski would have the responsibility of approving the plans or not, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The plan is approved by the chief of the General Staff; and if he is absent, this will be done by his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And, so, the G3 service, for example, during 2001, would have planned some operations, such as the operation around Vaksince, operations at Tetovo, operations at Aracinovo, et cetera, and discussed these plans with -- at the collegium. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For every single operation planned within G3, the collegium will discuss it; and, as I already mentioned, following the discussion at the collegium, the action is approved or the order is signed by the chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And Generals Petrovski and Stamboliski, they were experienced and competent military professional, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be incorrect by me to give assessments or evaluation about my superiors. Since your comment was a positive one, I can agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Well, then, I will take your answer as a yes. I'd like to turn to another topic, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm wondering whether we could take the second break now; otherwise, I will have to stop sort of in mid-topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Saxon. We can have the break now, and we will resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Markovski, yesterday, at page 10627 of the transcript, you said that: "In order to declare a state of war, three conditions have to be met," and this was in reference to Article 124 of the constitution. And the first condition that you mentioned was where you said there must be imminent danger posed to the Republic of Macedonia, and "this would mean attack coming from any of the neighbouring countries."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can, please, I would like to show the witness Exhibit P91, and that will be in binder 2, tab 51. I don't know what binder the witness has next to him. If he could be given binder 2, please, that would help, if that would assist him. For those looking on in e-court, Article 124 is at page 21 in the English version of e-court and page 25 in the Macedonian version of e-court. No, that is not the right document. We're looking for what should be P00091, which should be the constitution of Macedonia. There we are. And if we could go to page 21 in the English version and page 25 in the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you could turn, Dr. Markovski, to Article 124. Do you have that Article in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could go back one page in the English version, please, and if we could focus on Article 124.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The first of the three conditions that you mentioned yesterday, Dr. Markovski, you said there must be imminent danger posed to the Republic of Macedonia, and "this would mean attack coming from any of the -- this would mean attack coming from any of the neighbouring countries." Where do you see a requirement that the attack come from neighbouring countries within Article 124?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what other possibility there might be for a war threat. This means a danger or a threat of an organised military structure to the Republic of Macedonia. Military organisations or military structures are one of the basic attributes of every single country, and this is where I draw my conclusion from. There cannot be a military organisation without a country, nor a country without a military organisation as its own basic attribute, and I'm talking about democratic states.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, suppose there's an insurgent force that develops in a country. Can't an insurgent force be a military organisation or a military structure?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring me back to something that I already explained. In a democratic country, it is not logical that one might face such a situation. The problems in a democratic country are resolved through a political dialogue and through the institutions of the system. The Republic of Macedonia, regardless of the fact that it was at the very beginning of its democraticisation of its society, from the very beginning, it has established and built upon its democratic institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Markovski, take a look at that first provision, number 1 of Article 124. It reads like this: "A state of war exists when direct danger of military attack on the Republic is impending, or when the Republic is attacked, or war is declared on it." So that provision is written in the disjunctive construction, isn't it? It provides three different scenarios for a war, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, three conditions in order to declare a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you say it imposes three conditions, how do you explain the use of the words "or" in that first sentence?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: So there is one condition when there is an imminent danger. The second condition is, "or when the Republic is under attack." The third condition is when war has been declared on it. And this means, since we have this word "or" in between the three conditions, this means not every -- not all three conditions have to be met in order to declare state of war, but at least one and any of these three conditions in order to be able to declare a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Let's talk about maybe just the first condition for right now, when there is an imminent danger.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military. Imminent military or war danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Fine. Okay. Imminent danger of military attack or when the Republic is attacked. Let's talk about the first two conditions, if we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness what is Exhibit 1D0099, and this is at tab 9 of binder number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Markovski, this document is dated the 11th of June, 2001. It's a decision from President Trajkovski to establish the defence command of the city of Skopje. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it says that the 12th Infantry Brigade, the 16th Infantry Brigade, the 1st Guardist Brigade, and the 8th Infantry Brigade will be subordinate --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. It seems that I have another document then on the screen in front of me. Oh, very well. I apologise. Yes, in the second item, 12th, 16th, and so on. I apologise for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in item 3, it says that: "The chief of the General Staff of the army of the Republic of Macedonia will issue orders for engaging the units for the defence of the city of Skopje." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Doesn't this order, this decision, indicate that the Republic of Macedonia was in imminent military danger and was being attacked?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see this anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, what other conclusions would you draw from this?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this decision, it is not listed what is going on in the Republic of Macedonia or what the country is faced with. It just says that the training defence is supposed to establish a defence command for the city of Skopje, comprising these four-mentioned units and the Chief of Staff to make or adopt an order for the deployment of the units for the Defence of the city of Skopje, but it doesn't say from whom the city is supposed to defend and whether the city is facing this kind of threat. In accordance with the provisions of charter of the United Nations, Article 51, everything single country, that is including the Republic of Macedonia, will undertake appropriate measures in order to protect its territory from terrorists or asymmetrical activities, but also in cases as it is stipulated in the Article of the constitution that you have mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Markovski, isn't it logical that this order, this decision, was issued by the president due to the ongoing activities of the NLA inside the Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This order, this decision by the president has been made because of the disturbance of the security situation in the Republic of Macedonia as a result of the presence of armed extremist groups of ethnic Albanian composition in the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it`s true, isn't it, that a country can be attacked from within, can't it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The comparison that we are trying to make between the constitutional provisions and this decision is an inappropriate one. It says when there is an immediate danger, imminent danger of a military attack, and this can only happen from a military structure or institution. If we want to be specific, then the constitution should have read also asymmetrical threats for the security of the Republic of Macedonia, or, even more specific, possible terrorist activities inside the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you suggesting, Dr. Markovski, that when President Trajkovski issued this order on the 11th of June, that the city of Skopje was not in imminent danger of a military attack? Are you suggesting that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am trying to say that we could have had cases of infiltration of different terrorist groups, part of the armed extremist groups in the Republic of Macedonia, and this order was an order to prevent their infiltration in the city of Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, you see, that order doesn't say anything about preventing infiltration. But let me ask you this: Yesterday, at page 10679, you agreed with the proposition of my colleague, Ms. Residovic, that the defence of the capital city of the Republic of Macedonia is the most significant defence task of the armed forces and of the citizens of Macedonia. Do you recall that testimony from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are not the precise words I used; but, more or less, this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Well, then, if the armed forces of Macedonia needed to be mobilised in June 2001 to defend the capital city against the NLA, doesn't that sound like the Republic of Macedonia was in imminent danger?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this decision talks about prevention of infiltration and not about defence. The main task of the army is to prevent the infiltration or advancements of organised or non-organised groups or individuals with weaponry in the city where they would conduct and carry out their terrorist activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: First of all, Dr. Markovski, the word "infiltration" does not appear here in this document. Second of all, you haven't answered my question. My question was simple. I'll ask it again. If the armed forces needed to be mobilised in June 2001 to defend the capital city against the NLA, doesn't that sound like the Republic of Macedonia was in imminent danger?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But one cannot read in this decision that Skopje is under a military threat or military attack either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So the anticipate to my question is no, then.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I cannot accept this kind of an answer. This was a decision made in the sense of prevention. Because I am familiar with the situation, I know what were the preconditions. So it was a decision in order to prevent the penetration of armed extremists groups and individuals in the city where they would carry out certain terrorist activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Markovski, at page 10621 of the transcript, yesterday, you told the Trial Chamber that the NLA, in 2001, was trying to create a situation "where they would be able to control one portion of the territory of the Republic of Macedonia and, with additional attempts, to establish their own political power on this territory." And my question for is this: If units or groups of the NLA were pushing close to the city of Skopje by June of 2001, doesn't had a sound like the NLA was close to reaching its goal by that time, the goal that you described to us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The infiltration of armed extremists in Skopje and their intention to carry out terrorist activities doesn't mean this. At the end of the day, the best example would be Teli's group where the Ministry of Interior, that is to say, the structures within the MOI, dealt with this problem and resolved this issue with the terrorist group in a very quick manner. So by entering of these structures into the city, it doesn't mean that it is under a military threat, but the city can find itself in a situation where terrorist activities would be carried out inside the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Markovski, by June of 2001, the NLA was in control of the village or the suburb of Aracinovo. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, doesn't that sound like that and doesn't that indicate that, by coming so close to Skopje by June of 2001 and controlling territories so close to Skopje, that the NLA was quite close to accomplishing the goal, or the goals, that you described yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not, at least for Skopje. The entry of the armed extremist group in Aracinovo, and the period until the moment when they were forced out of the village, was ten to 12 days. If Macedonia, that is to say, the security forces of the Republic, if they wanted to resolve this problem at the very first day and information was available, they could have done so, but we would have had plenty of victims and destruction. So it would have not been effective, so the principle of effectiveness would not have been satisfied. And the Republic of Macedonia did not opt for destruction and killing, but, most of all, to use political means to resolve the situation. And, of course, whenever we had serious problems, the president would make the decision to apply and deploy the security forces. This has been done only on six occasions through decisions of the president, and only five of them have been implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just to clarify your response, you said that if the Macedonian security forces had resolved the problem in Aracinovo on its own, on the very first day, they could have done so, but there would have been plenty victims and destruction. It's fair to say, isn't it, that, by June 2001, it was pretty predictable that military operations in populated areas - for example, like Aracinovo - would result in lots of victims and lots of destruction? Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that one cannot generalise the situation. There were 260 armed extremists in Aracinovo, and this was a fact known to the police and the army. This is not a force that one should fear from, the police or the army for that matter. So the resource effectiveness is what matters because the Republic of Macedonia was always following the notion that we have to continue living together, and this applies for -- to all the citizens in the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. You said, a moment ago, that the security forces, if they had want to the resolve this problem, they could have done so, the problem in Aracinovo. Why was the occupation of Aracinovo by the NLA a problem for the state?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any square metre, if the situation there is not safe and secure, is a problem for the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you say the situation - for example, in Aracinovo - was not safe and secure, it was not safe and secure because the NLA, at that moment, controlled Aracinovo, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not the NLA, it was a group composed of around 260 armed extremists. Sometimes, the reason should be prevail over the violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we agree, Dr. Markovski, that the groups of armed extremists that were carrying out armed violence in 2001 went by the name or the acronym the NLA? Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why, then, do you say that the group composed of around 260 armed extremists who took control of Aracinovo was not the NLA?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I don't think that the NLA existed at all under this acronym, something is being represented as an armed structure while it did not exist at all. There were several armed extremists groups that neither had a joint plan of action nor they implemented any coordinated activity. Each of these armed extremist groups carried out their actions according to their own plans and views.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, we're going to come back to this then. Yesterday, at page 10628 of the transcript, you told us that the president can declare a state of war in a situation where the parliament cannot meet or convene. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In such a case, the president has one additional competence within the competencies vested in him by the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you also explained yesterday that, during the crisis, the parliament was in permanent session, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and this is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we go back to what is exhibit P00091, please, the constitution of the Republic of Macedonia, and if we can go back to Article 124, please. Again, this is at tab 51 in the second binder. And Article 124 on e-court should be at page 20 or 21 in the English version and page 25 in the Macedonian version, and if we can focus on article 124, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You'll see, Doctor, that paragraph 2 of Article 124 says that: "A state of war is declared by the Assembly," by the parliament, "by a two-thirds majority vote of the total number of representatives of the Assembly, on the proposal of the president of the Republic, the government, or at least 30 representatives." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In peace," it is specifically stated, and this is properly stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So what that means is, during 2001, either the president, the government, or at least 30 representatives of parliament could have proposed that a state of war be declared, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, for example, there were times during the crisis period when the prime minister, Ljubco Georgievski, argued that a state of war should be declared. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read that information as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Markovski, wasn't the real reason that a state of war was never declared, back in 2001, was that the result would have been a full-scale civil war between the ethnic Macedonian and the ethnic Albanian communities in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I really did not understand the question. Could you simply it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, it's probably my fault. It's okay. The result of the declaration of a state of war, or the consequence of the declaration of a state of war in 2001, would have been a full-scale civil war between the ethnic Macedonian and the ethnic Albanian communities in Macedonia, and so isn't that the real reason why a state of war was formally never declared?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You could make such assertion but that would be conjecture only, and I have a correction to enter. As you said, it would be a war between the ethnic Albanian population and all the others, because all the others did not join the armed extremist groups of the Albanians in the Republic of Macedonia. When I'm speaking about all the others, I'm referring to the fact that in the Republic of Macedonia, in addition to the Macedonians and Albanians, there are also ethnic Serbs, Bosniak, Turks, Roma, Vlachs, and Serbs, and I hope the other ethnicities that I have not mentioned will not mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. You say that my proposition could be made but that it would only be conjecture, but I'm asking you really for your expert opinion. You're here testifying as an expert, as a political/military expert. So I'd like, really, a clearer answer to my question. Isn't the really reason why with a state of war was never formally declared was because the consequence would have been a full-scale civil war?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are really trying to make me oppose you, because the science is not based on conjecture. The science is based on events and documents. So from the scientific aspect, I really wouldn't like to enter any conjectures. I apologise, but, really, such conjecture is not something that I can accept at face value. I need to have arguments, I need to have scientific knowledge and researches to then arrive at any conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Markovski, you were, in light of the position that you held in the Ministry of Defence in 2001, you were a witness to those events; you were, at times, a participant in those events; you've spent many years now studying those events, teaching about them. So I'm asking to you give your expert opinion, please.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I was not a participant; I was a witness to those. And I remain at my position, that it is very difficult to guess what would happen if something else would happen; but probably, and let me satisfy your need for the answer, probably, having learned from the experiences from the immediate neighbourhood and particularly the events of Bosnia-Herzegovina but also Croatia, probably, there would have been a large bloodshed. But still, still, I'm just giving you this answer to provide an answer to the question; and, otherwise, I do not fully stand from a scientific aspect behind this answer and this conjecture.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. It's true, isn't it, that in 2001 the security forces of Macedonia were operating in an undeclared state of war, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: During a certain period, during the crisis in 2001, they lived and worked in a situation of increased battle readiness. It has been precisely defined, and this is how they acted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the security forces also lived and worked in a situation of combat, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That would be too harsh an assertion, which is not based in the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll come back to that in a minute. I'd like to move to a different topic now. Dr. Markovski, do you have a binder there with your report in it? Do you have a copy of your report with you? Because if not, we can give you one.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have my report here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. All right. If you go to paragraph 21, please, of your report -- actually, I'm going to direct you to a different paragraph. I'm sorry. Dr. Markovski, could you turn to paragraph 24, please. In paragraph 24, you provide some definitions of the word "crisis." First, you say: "Crisis is the disruption of certain rules and norms that function in the specific system. Crisis is a national or international situation which presents a threat to the vital interests of the country." Then, later on, you cite it a document in footnote 11 -- excuse me, footnote 12. Actually, you cite to your own work, to your own book? Then, in the middle of the paragraph, there's a sentence beginning with: "The NATO handbook defines ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says: "The NATO handbook defines crisis as a network of rapidly evolving events that significantly increase the influence of the destabilizing factors in the broader international system, or, one of its subsystems, above the normal level, an increase the probability of the onset of violence; 2, the continuation of consequences of actions between the governments of two or more sore republican states and specific convicts, a short and real war which can escalate into a large dangerous war; 3, a change in the status that is characterised by an increase in the likelihood of destructive actions between two or more opponents with a high probability of military action." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And as authority for that definition, you cite in footnote 13 to the NATO handbook, chapter on the strategic concept of the alliance that starts at page 42.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The strategic concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn please to what is 65 ter number 2D00-713, please. This is the NATO handbook, or a portion of it, from 2001. It's in binder 3, tab 67. And, perhaps, if the witness could be given binder 3 and directed to this tab, it might make things easier for him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We only have this in English, and if we could turn to page 42, please, of the NATO handbook.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Markovski, you'll see at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, can we scroll counsel to the bottom of the page. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You'll see, here, we have this chapter that you've cited here for the definition of a crisis. The chapter is called: The strategic concept of the alliance. It's about five or six pages long. Can you tell us please where we will finds the definition of crisis that you mention here in the middle of paragraph 24, which page?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: So if we wish to be really proper about what is mentioned in paragraph 21 and everything that is mentioned here, it reads --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Paragraph 24, you mean.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 24.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 24 of my report, it reads that: "In the NATO handbook, the definition of crisis is what has been indicated," and then number 1, number 2, number 3. Nothing of this is placed under quotation marks. It is allowed - I don't know how it is in the law - but in the science, it is permissible when running analysis to be able to draw conclusions and then present those conclusions as one's own, but they are not then placed under quotation marks. So, what has been indicated here in the strategic concept of the NATO alliance, in pages 42 to 47, as my view, I have made these three conclusions and I am presenting them here without quotation marks. So these were my conclusions from the materials that I have studied, analysed, and, therefore, reached those conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Look, we've got some time. It is only five or six pages. I understand that you haven't quoted this chapter precisely, but where in these pages do you see a discussion of what a crisis is? Where do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have here just the English version. I don't know whether the Macedonian version is available as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sorry. We only have the English version. I do believe you read the English language, and you cited to this in your report.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am able to use the English language; but to be able to make a professional analysis, I still need the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, since you can use the English language, can you turn -- can you just look at these pages and see if the word "crisis" is there.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are really making me, again, to analyse something from the top of my head. I did permit myself to answer your question using conjecture, but I really wouldn't like to run an analysis based on a language that I do not fully understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The truth is, there's no discussion of what a crisis is in this chapter of the handbook, is there?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is the conclusion you make, then so be it. I can't make an analysis from a language that I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time. Should we end for the day now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will consider that. Now we must ask you, sir, to return again tomorrow to continue. We resume again at 9.00 in the morning. The court officer will show you out now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, I thought, in the absence of the witness, we might inquire how you saw your timing. We are not holding to you minutes. Days would be a start.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I was afraid of that. My objective, Your Honour, is to finish my cross-examination by the end of the day on Thursday. That is my objective. I see Judge Van den Wyngaert is not happy with that, but this witness covers a huge amount of material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I think we might encourage to you finish earlier than that, Mr. Saxon, at least by the end of the second session on Thursday, with a view to Mr. Apostolski having the complete last session on Thursday, because of commitments that would make it hard for two of the Judges now to be present on Friday. And if that isn't the case, it would disrupt the flow of things. But if you look at the time fully available tomorrow and for two of the three sessions on Thursday, it ought to give you plenty of scope to deal adequately, I would think, with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We would be grateful if you could attempt that. The Chamber would also mention that, for another or for a related issue that affects me, I'm having to be engaged in other matters both on Friday and on Monday of next week; and for that reason, we would propose for the last or the one remaining witness of Mr. Apostolski to deal with that witness on Tuesday, rather than simply have two Judges sit and hear that witness. And given the fact that it is a 92 bis witness and there is essentially only cross-examination, we should be able to finish that witness on Tuesday and deal with any procedural matters that are then to be dealt with, with a view to concluding your evidentiary sittings on Tuesday of next week. Strength to your planning and preparation for the next day and two-thirds, Mr. Saxon. We will adjourn now and resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 12th day of March, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
